case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a defendant’s broad plea-agreement appeal waiver bars an appellate challenge to a supervised-release condition on due-process grounds, and whether the waiver becomes unenforceable when the sentencing judge later tells the defendant he has a right to appeal and the government does not object.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. § 1343 (wire fraud) and 18 U.S.C. § 2 (aiding and abetting) (underlying conviction); the enforceability of plea-agreement appeal waivers as a matter of federal criminal procedure/contract-like plea principles; Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment (as the asserted basis for challenging the supervised-release condition).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Hunter argues that the Fifth Circuit wrongly enforced his general appeal waiver to dismiss an appeal raising a due-process challenge to a future supervised-release condition, contending that (1) appeal waivers should not be limited to only two exceptions (ineffective assistance and sentence above the statutory maximum) and should allow review of at least certain fundamental/constitutional sentencing errors, and (2) even if the waiver would ordinarily apply, it should not be enforced where the district judge affirmatively advised at sentencing that Hunter had a right to appeal and the government failed to object—creating (at minimum) ambiguity or reliance incompatible with treating the waiver as knowing/voluntary and enforceable.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States argues the Fifth Circuit correctly dismissed because Hunter knowingly and voluntarily waived his right to appeal on all grounds except ineffective assistance of counsel, and that waiver covers challenges to supervised-release conditions (including constitutional/due-process challenges) unless they fall within a recognized exception; the government further argues the district court’s boilerplate, unobjected-to statement at the close of sentencing that Hunter had a right to appeal does not negate or modify an otherwise valid waiver and does not create an enforceability problem warranting Supreme Court intervention.

Margalli-Olvera v. INS, 43 F.3d 345 (8th Cir. 1994)
Jones v. United States, cert. denied, No. 24-6505 (June 6, 2025)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the best point: a sentencing judge’s unqualified Rule 32(j) advisement, plus prosecutorial silence, can create practical ambiguity and reliance at the moment the defendant must decide whether to appeal. But under a minimal, administrable rule consistent with Ricketts, the enforceability of an appeal waiver turns on whether it was knowing and voluntary at the Rule 11 plea colloquy, and a generic Rule 32(j) script is most reasonably read—as Justice Kagan argues—as describing only whatever limited appellate rights remain, not as a mutual modification of the bargain. Garza affects the analysis by confirming waivers are not absolute (and counsel may still have duties), yet it does not empower courts to treat routine post-sentencing advisements as undoing otherwise valid waivers absent a clear indication of modification or a defect in the plea itself. Adopting petitioner’s reliance theory would invite instability by turning boilerplate sentencing language into a broad exception, whereas we can preserve fairness through existing channels (challenges to the waiver’s validity, ambiguity in the waiver’s text, or ineffective-assistance claims) without rewriting plea agreements.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the strongest objection—reliance-based ambiguity from the Rule 32(j) advisement plus prosecutorial silence—but that theory cannot overcome the controlling texts: the written waiver and the Rule 11 colloquy confirming it was knowing and voluntary at the time of assent. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan explain, Rule 32(j) is best read as a mandatory notice of whatever appellate rights remain, not a judicial power to modify a plea agreement absent mutual assent, and the government’s silence in response to boilerplate does not supply that assent under our contract-like plea precedents such as Ricketts. Garza v. Idaho, invoked by Sotomayor and Jackson, is relevant only to counsel’s duty to file a notice of appeal despite a waiver; it does not create a due-process-based exception that nullifies clear waiver language whenever a standard advisement is given. Because no constitutional or statutory text requires the extra exception petitioner seeks, I would enforce the waiver according to its terms and affirm.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson’s reliance/ambiguity theory has equitable appeal, but it fails under the governing texts: the plea agreement’s waiver and the Rule 11 colloquy are what establish a knowing and voluntary relinquishment, and a boilerplate Rule 32(j) advisement is best read—as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan explain—as describing whatever limited appellate rights remain, not as a modification requiring mutual assent. Garza v. Idaho, which Sotomayor and Jackson invoke, concerns counsel’s duty to file a notice of appeal notwithstanding a waiver and presupposes that waivers remain generally enforceable as to claims; it does not empower courts to treat routine end-of-sentencing scripts (and prosecutorial silence before any issue crystallizes) as vitiating clear waiver language. Treating such advisements as waiver-nullifying would invite strategic appeals and destabilize plea bargaining, contrary to the contract-like enforcement principles reflected in Ricketts and the practical need for finality. Absent facial ambiguity in the waiver or a concrete defect in the plea’s voluntariness, I would enforce the waiver according to its terms, including as to supervised-release conditions repackaged as due-process claims.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan persuasively argue that a Rule 32(j) advisement is best read as describing whatever appeal rights remain and cannot “unilaterally amend” a plea bargain, and I agree we should not treat boilerplate as a judicial rewrite. But that framing still leaves my core concern unanswered: enforceability depends not just on what was said at Rule 11 in the abstract, but on whether the system’s own on-the-record instructions at the critical moment for filing an appeal (and the government’s silence) create a reasonable, reliance-based ambiguity about what rights survived, undermining the knowing-and-voluntary predicate as applied. Garza v. Idaho, as Justice Jackson emphasizes, does not make post-sentencing advisements dispositive, but it confirms waivers are not monolithic and that appellate rights retain independent procedural significance—supporting a narrow rule that we do not enforce a waiver to block review of supervised-release conditions when the court affirmatively tells the defendant he has a right to appeal without clarification. Contract analogies (Ricketts) do not eliminate the due-process problem of official misinformation in open court; my approach does not “modify” the bargain, it construes enforceability against forfeiture where the record injects materially misleading ambiguity at the moment rights must be exercised.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the hardest point: the judge’s unequivocal “right to appeal” statement, plus prosecutorial silence, may generate practical reliance-based ambiguity at the moment the defendant must decide whether to appeal. But on a pragmatic textualist account, the workable reading—consistent with Chief Justice Roberts’s framing—is that Rule 32(j)(1)(B) requires advising the defendant of whatever appellate rights remain after a Rule 11-confirmed waiver, not that a routine advisement retroactively destabilizes a written bargain absent clear mutual assent. Garza, as Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett note, presupposes enforceable waivers and addresses notice/ineffective-assistance dynamics; it does not supply a doctrinal bridge from boilerplate sentencing script to nullification of a clear waiver term. Treating silence at sentencing as modification would make waiver enforceability hinge on predictable boilerplate and opportunistic non-objection, undermining statutory/rule coherence and plea-bargaining stability without a strong textual hook.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson press the hardest point: that the judge’s unequivocal Rule 32(j)-style advisement plus government silence creates reliance-based ambiguity at the moment a notice of appeal must be filed. But under a textualist, contract-like framework (as the Chief Justice and Justice Kagan emphasize), the operative assent is the written waiver and the Rule 11 colloquy establishing it was knowing and voluntary; a later, generic advisement is best read as describing whatever residual rights remain and cannot unilaterally modify the bargain absent mutual assent. Garza does not supply a doctrine that boilerplate advisements negate clear waivers—it addresses counsel’s duty to file and acknowledges some claims survive, not that sentencing scripts rewrite agreements. Accepting petitioner’s reliance theory would effectively empower courts (and silence by the prosecutor) to alter negotiated plea terms after the fact, a result in tension with separation of powers and our contract-enforcement precedents like Ricketts.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson present the strongest opposing point: that a Rule 32(j) advisement plus government silence creates reliance-based ambiguity at the critical moment for deciding whether to appeal. But under the contract-like framework reflected in Ricketts and the Rule 11 focus on whether the waiver was knowing and voluntary when made, a generic post-sentencing statement is best read (as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan argue) to refer to whatever limited appellate rights remain notwithstanding the waiver, not as a modification requiring mutual assent. Garza—invoked by Sotomayor and Jackson—confirms waivers are not absolute and some claims survive, but it does not establish that boilerplate sentencing advisements nullify an otherwise valid waiver or retroactively make it unknowing. Adopting petitioner’s reliance rule would make waiver enforceability turn on routine scripts and non-objection, destabilizing plea bargaining and inviting post hoc uncertainty without a clear doctrinal or textual hook.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson’s reliance-based ambiguity argument is the strongest counter, but under a textualist, Rule-anchored approach the “knowing and voluntary” inquiry attaches to the plea agreement and the Rule 11 colloquy that crystallizes assent, not to a later Rule 32(j) advisement that is routinely phrased and best read—as Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan explain—as describing whatever residual appellate rights remain. Government silence at sentencing is not mutual assent to modify a written waiver, and treating boilerplate post-sentencing script as an implied amendment would undermine the contract-like stability we have emphasized in cases like Ricketts and invite after-the-fact uncertainty. Garza, as several colleagues note, concerns counsel’s duty to file a notice of appeal and the fact that waivers are not monolithic, but it does not suggest that standard judicial advisements retroactively nullify a clear waiver absent a defect in the plea’s voluntariness. Because petitioner points to no ambiguity in the waiver’s text and no Rule 11 deficiency, I would enforce the waiver as written.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: I accept Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kagan’s core point that a Rule 32(j) advisement cannot, by itself, unilaterally amend a plea waiver as a matter of contract-like enforcement under Ricketts. But my position is not that the waiver was rewritten—it is that the court’s unequivocal statement that the defendant had a “right to appeal,” combined with the government’s silence, creates a material, state-generated ambiguity at the precise moment the defendant must decide whether to invoke appellate process, which bears on the fairness of enforcing forfeiture in this posture. Justice Gorsuch’s reliance on Class and the idea that the government can wait to invoke the waiver later doesn’t answer the due-process concern that official misinformation can reasonably induce non-action and thereby erode the practical premise of a knowing, fair relinquishment of review for supervised-release conditions affecting liberty. Garza reinforces for me that waivers are not absolute and that appellate rights retain structural significance; it supports a pragmatic, procedurally fair rule resolving this kind of court-created ambiguity against strict waiver enforcement here.

John Roberts.reasoning: A knowing and voluntary appellate waiver in a plea agreement is generally enforceable according to its terms under contract-like plea principles, see Ricketts v. Adamson, 483 U.S. 1 (1987), and Hunter’s waiver broadly covered sentencing challenges, including supervised-release conditions, absent an agreed-upon exception. The district court’s Rule 32(j)-style advisement at sentencing that Hunter had a “right to appeal” does not unilaterally amend the bargain or negate the earlier knowing waiver; at most it accurately described whatever limited appellate rights remained, and the government’s silence does not supply mutual assent to modification. Garza v. Idaho, 586 U.S. 232 (2019), underscores that waivers do not extinguish every possible claim, but it does not hold that a post-sentencing advisement invalidates an otherwise valid waiver or creates a new right to appeal. To preserve institutional legitimacy and avoid creating a broad, uncertain exception for post hoc sentencing colloquies, I would enforce the waiver on narrow grounds and affirm dismissal.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: A knowing and voluntary plea agreement is enforceable according to its terms, and a broad waiver of the right to appeal “on all grounds” encompasses challenges to supervised-release conditions, including constitutional objections, unless the waiver itself reserves that issue; nothing in the text of the Fifth Amendment or the federal plea framework creates a freestanding due-process exception to an otherwise valid waiver. This Court has treated plea agreements as contract-like instruments that bind both parties when entered knowingly and voluntarily, see Ricketts v. Adamson, 483 U.S. 1 (1987), and Garza v. Idaho, 586 U.S. 232 (2019), while recognizing only that waivers are not absolute without prescribing additional mandatory exceptions. The district court’s post-sentencing boilerplate statement that the defendant “has a right to appeal,” without more, does not rewrite the parties’ bargain or nullify the waiver, and the government’s failure to object cannot supply contractual modification or constitutional defect where the waiver’s text remains clear. Enforcing the waiver respects the agreement’s original public meaning and preserves the limited, bargained-for nature of appellate review in the plea context.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: A plea-agreement appeal waiver is generally enforceable when it is knowing and voluntary, and it can encompass even constitutional claims unless Congress or the Constitution provides an affirmative indication to the contrary. See Ricketts v. Adamson, 483 U.S. 1, 8-10 (1987); cf. Garza v. Idaho, 586 U.S. 232, 238-239 (2019). Nothing in the Due Process Clause or the wire-fraud statutes (18 U.S.C. §§ 1343, 2) requires creating a special carveout for supervised-release-condition challenges that a defendant expressly waived, and enforcing waivers serves practical interests in finality and efficient administration of justice. The district judge’s boilerplate post-sentencing statement about a “right to appeal,” unaccompanied by any clear modification of the written bargain, should not vitiate the waiver; otherwise routine misstatements would undermine negotiated pleas and invite strategic appeals despite the waiver.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: A broad appeal waiver cannot be treated as a “monolithic end to all appellate rights,” and defendants must retain meaningful ability to contest whether the waiver is valid and enforceable in the circumstances, including whether later events rendered any purported relinquishment unknowing or involuntary. Garza v. Idaho, 586 U.S. 232 (2019), recognizes that at least some claims are unwaivable and, most fundamentally, that defendants may challenge the waiver’s validity; here, the sentencing judge’s affirmative advisement that Hunter had a right to appeal—coupled with the government’s silence—creates at minimum a reliance-based ambiguity incompatible with strict enforcement of the waiver. Given the real-world stakes of supervised-release conditions and their direct impact on liberty, due-process challenges to such conditions should not be summarily foreclosed by boilerplate waivers when the court’s own statements reasonably suggested continued appellate review. Contract-like plea principles (Ricketts v. Adamson, 483 U.S. 1 (1987)) do not justify enforcing a waiver in a manner that undermines fairness and the knowing, voluntary nature required for relinquishing constitutional rights.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: A knowing and voluntary appeal waiver is generally enforceable according to its terms, and nothing in Rule 11 or ordinary plea-agreement principles permits a district court to unilaterally rewrite that bargain at the end of sentencing. Under Ricketts v. Adamson, plea agreements are enforced in a contract-like way, and the judge’s generic Rule 32(j)(1)(B) advisement that the defendant has a “right to appeal” is best read as referring to whatever limited appellate rights remain after the waiver, not as an amendment. Garza v. Idaho recognizes that the government can forfeit reliance on a waiver, but mere silence in the face of a boilerplate advisement—without any mutual assent or clear relinquishment—does not, as a workable rule, create a new appellate right or make the waiver unenforceable. Because the waiver broadly covers sentencing and supervised-release challenges and the due-process claim does not fall within a recognized exception, the Fifth Circuit properly dismissed.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: A plea agreement is a contract-like instrument, and its appeal waiver should be enforced according to its plain terms when entered knowingly and voluntarily; nothing in the Due Process Clause or federal plea procedure creates a freestanding exception allowing appellate review of supervised-release conditions simply because the challenge is framed as constitutional. The district court’s post-sentencing Rule 32(j)-style advisement that the defendant has a right to appeal cannot rewrite the bargain the parties struck, and the government’s failure to object at that moment is not a forfeiture because the proper time to invoke the waiver is after a notice of appeal and the issues are known. Garza v. Idaho confirms that appeal waivers do not eliminate all appellate rights, but it likewise treats waivers as generally enforceable and does not suggest that a generic advisement at sentencing negates an otherwise valid waiver; similarly, Class v. United States shows that judicial misstatements do not themselves manufacture or extinguish waiver terms. Enforcing the waiver here respects the parties’ agreement and avoids judicial alteration of negotiated terms, consistent with separation-of-powers limits on courts revising plea bargains.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: A knowing and voluntary plea-agreement appeal waiver is generally enforceable and should be applied according to its terms, including to challenges to supervised-release conditions, absent a recognized exception; that approach accords with the Court’s longstanding treatment of plea agreements as binding, contract-like instruments. See Ricketts v. Adamson, 483 U.S. 1 (1987). The district court’s post-sentencing Rule 32(j)(1)(B) advisement that the defendant had a “right to appeal” does not unilaterally modify the parties’ bargain or negate an otherwise valid waiver, particularly where Rule 11 supplied the relevant safeguards at the time of the plea and there was no mutual assent to amendment. Enforcing the waiver here also serves practical workability and the stability of plea bargaining, while leaving intact established avenues for review (e.g., ineffective-assistance claims), as reflected in Garza v. Idaho, 586 U.S. 232 (2019).

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: A plea agreement’s appeal waiver is enforceable when its text, read in ordinary contract-like fashion, clearly covers “any appeal” except specified carveouts, and Hunter’s due-process challenge to a supervised-release condition falls within that broad language. This Court has recognized that defendants may knowingly and voluntarily waive even constitutional and appellate rights as part of a plea bargain, and nothing in the Due Process Clause or the relevant statutes (18 U.S.C. §§ 1343, 2) supplies an “affirmative indication” that such waiver is categorically unavailable. Garza v. Idaho confirms that an appeal waiver limits the claims a defendant may pursue on appeal, even if it does not extinguish counsel’s ministerial duty to file a notice when instructed; it does not suggest that a judge’s post-sentencing boilerplate advisement, unaccompanied by any modification of the plea’s terms, nullifies an otherwise valid waiver. Absent ambiguity in the waiver itself or a showing that the plea was unknowing or involuntary, the later statement about a “right to appeal” does not rewrite the parties’ bargain, and precedent’s emphasis on enforcing plea agreements counsels dismissal.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Although plea-agreement appeal waivers are generally enforceable when entered knowingly and voluntarily, plea bargains are only “contract-like,” and their enforcement must remain consistent with basic procedural fairness and due process. Where the sentencing judge affirmatively advises the defendant—on the record at sentencing—that he has a right to appeal, and the government does not object, that official pronouncement creates at least material ambiguity about the continued scope/enforceability of the waiver and undermines the premise that the waiver is being applied in a knowing, voluntary, and fair manner. Garza v. Idaho, 586 U.S. 232 (2019), recognizes both the contract analogy and the continuing significance of appellate rights even in the presence of a waiver, supporting a rule that courts should not mechanically enforce broad waivers when later court conduct reasonably induces reliance to the contrary. Given the practical consequences in the supervised-release context—where conditions can implicate core liberty interests and due-process concerns—I would allow the appeal to proceed rather than treating the waiver as an absolute bar.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a defendant’s broad appeal waiver remains enforceable (and bars appellate review) when he challenges a supervised-release condition on due-process grounds and when the sentencing judge later states—without government objection—that the defendant has a right to appeal.
case_analysis.legal_provision: 18 U.S.C. § 1343 (wire fraud affecting a financial institution) and 18 U.S.C. § 2 (aiding and abetting) as the conviction statutes; the enforceability of appeal waivers arises from federal plea-agreement doctrine (contract-like principles under Federal Rule of Criminal Procedure 11) and the Due Process Clause as applied to the challenged supervised-release condition.
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Hunter argues that the Fifth Circuit wrongly treated appeal waivers as nearly absolute—limited only to ineffective-assistance claims or sentences above the statutory maximum—and that his due-process challenge to a condition of future supervised release should be appealable notwithstanding the waiver. He also contends the waiver should not be enforced because the district court advised him at sentencing that he had a right to appeal and the government did not object, which (in his view) undermines the knowing/voluntary nature of the waiver or constitutes a modification/forfeiture preventing the government from invoking it.
case_analysis.respondent_position: The United States argues the appeal waiver was knowing and voluntary and expressly covers any appeal on any ground other than ineffective assistance, so it bars Hunter’s due-process challenge to a supervised-release condition. The government also argues that the district court’s routine, unobjected-to statement at the end of sentencing that Hunter had a right to appeal does not negate or alter the earlier Rule 11-confirmed waiver in the plea agreement, and thus the Fifth Circuit correctly dismissed the appeal.

Ricketts v. Adamson, 483 U.S. 1 (1987)
Abney v. United States, 431 U.S. 651 (1977)
Albrecht v. United States, 329 U.S. 599 (1947)
Margalli-Olvera v. INS, 43 F.3d 345 (8th Cir. 1994)

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Jackson’s procedural-fairness argument—that the Rule 32(j) advisement plus the government’s silence creates reasonable reliance or forfeiture—most directly tests my view, but it still cannot overcome the Rule 11 record establishing a knowing and voluntary waiver and the settled principle (reflected in Ricketts v. Adamson) that modifying a plea bargain requires mutual assent, not a routine ministerial notice. Justice Sotomayor’s concern about insulating serious supervised-release conditions from review is weighty, yet Garza v. Idaho’s statement that waivers are not “absolute” preserves narrow, established exceptions (invalid waiver, breach, lack of authority), and it does not authorize a free-floating due-process carveout whenever a condition affects future liberty. As Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch emphasize, treating standardized Rule 32(j) advisements as implied amendments would destabilize plea practice and invite litigation over colloquy wording rather than waiver validity and scope. A narrow holding enforcing this waiver on this record—without opining on the condition’s constitutionality and without foreclosing challenges that fit recognized exceptions—best protects administrability and the Court’s institutional legitimacy.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s due-process “carveout” argument and Justice Jackson’s reliance/forfeiture theory both ask us to override the waiver’s text based on equitable concerns untethered to the Constitution’s original public meaning; there is no freestanding, unwaivable constitutional right to appellate review. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan explain, Garza v. Idaho recognizes only limited, established exceptions (invalid waiver, breach, lack of authority) and does not transform a routine Rule 32(j) advisement into an alteration of a Rule 11-confirmed plea bargain. Under Ricketts v. Adamson’s contract-like framework, modification requires mutual assent, and the government’s silence during a standardized advisement cannot rewrite a material term already accepted on the record. Because the waiver’s validity is not impeached here, enforcing it respects the bargain and avoids creating an atextual constitutional exception for any claim labeled “due process.”

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor and Justice Jackson raise the most serious concern: that enforcing this waiver, especially after the Rule 32(j) advisement and government silence, could functionally insulate a potentially unconstitutional supervised-release condition from review and undermine procedural fairness. But under the text of the waiver (“any appeal on any ground” except ineffective assistance) and the Rule 11 record confirming it was knowing and voluntary, due process does not authorize us to create an atextual carveout for claims styled as “due process,” nor to treat a standardized Rule 32 notice as amending a plea bargain. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan explain, Garza preserves only established exceptions (invalid waiver, breach, lack of authority), and Ricketts v. Adamson’s contract-like framework makes clear that modification requires mutual assent, which a routine advisement and silence do not supply. Practical consequences reinforce that conclusion: letting ministerial advisements nullify bargained-for waivers would destabilize plea practice and invite strategic end-runs around comprehensive waivers.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts is right that a routine Rule 32(j) advisement should not generally “rewrite” a knowing and voluntary Rule 11 waiver, and I would not adopt any rule that destabilizes plea practice on that basis alone. But Justice Jackson correctly reframes the problem as one of procedural fairness and reasonable reliance at the critical sentencing moment: the court affirmatively told the defendant he retained a right to appeal, and the government’s silence in that exchange makes enforcement of the waiver against this particular challenge look less like honoring a bargain and more like springing a trap. Ricketts v. Adamson’s contract analogy, emphasized by Justice Kagan and Justice Gorsuch, cannot do all the work where what is at stake is ongoing future restraint on liberty and bodily integrity via supervised-release conditions, and where the record at sentencing affirmatively undermines the clarity on which “knowing” relinquishment depends in practice. Garza v. Idaho does not create a free-floating carveout, but it does underscore that broad waivers are not absolute and, in my view, due process permits at least appellate review of whether a supervised-release condition of this seriousness is lawful when the defendant was told on the record he could appeal.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Jackson’s reliance-based fairness argument—that the Rule 32(j) advisement plus the government’s silence created a reasonable understanding of an appeal right—has real equitable pull, but it cannot overcome the waiver’s unqualified text (“any appeal on any ground” except ineffective assistance) and the Rule 11 record confirming it was knowing and voluntary at the time of assent. Under the contract-like framework the Chief Justice and Justice Barrett invoke (Ricketts v. Adamson), modification of a material plea term requires mutual assent; a standardized post-sentencing notice is not an offer to amend, and silence in response to a ministerial advisement is not acceptance. Justice Sotomayor’s due-process concern about insulating supervised-release conditions from review is serious, yet Garza v. Idaho (as Justice Roberts and Justice Gorsuch note) preserves only established exceptions—invalid waiver, breach, or lack of authority—and does not create a categorical carveout for any claim framed as due process. The administrable, text-coherent rule is to enforce the waiver while leaving open those traditional safety valves and any collateral avenues Congress has provided for later challenges to ongoing conditions.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Sotomayor’s due-process concern about insulating burdensome supervised-release conditions from review is the hardest point, but it asks us to invent an extra-textual, claim-specific exception to a waiver whose scope was confirmed under Rule 11 as knowing and voluntary. Justice Jackson’s reliance-and-government-silence theory likewise cannot prevail because Rule 32(j)(1)(B) is a mandatory, standardized advisement that does not purport to amend plea terms, and under Ricketts v. Adamson contract-like modification requires mutual assent—not silence in response to a ministerial notice after the court has accepted the bargain. Garza v. Idaho, as Justice Kagan and the Chief Justice explain, preserves only limited categories (invalid waiver, breach, proceedings beyond authority) and does not convert Rule 32’s advisement into an implied rewriting of an explicit appellate waiver. Under a principled textualist/originalist approach, the proper course is to enforce the waiver as written while leaving intact established safety valves for genuinely unlawful sentences beyond the court’s power or invalid waivers.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Jackson’s procedural-fairness point—that a Rule 32(j) advisement plus the government’s silence creates reasonable reliance or forfeiture—is the strongest push against enforcement, but it does not overcome the Rule 11 record establishing a knowing and voluntary waiver or supply the mutual assent required to modify a plea agreement under Ricketts v. Adamson. As Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan emphasize, Garza v. Idaho does not create an open-ended constitutional carveout for due-process challenges; it preserves narrow, established routes (invalid waiver, breach, sentence beyond authority), and none is shown here. Justice Sotomayor’s concern about insulating serious supervised-release conditions from review is weighty, but under an institutionalist, administrable approach we cannot treat standardized, post-sentencing advisements as silently nullifying bargained-for waivers across the federal system. The proper limiting principle remains enforcing waivers as written while leaving intact the existing safety valves for unlawfulness that goes to the court’s power or the waiver’s validity.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Jackson’s reliance/forfeiture theory is the most serious challenge, but under Rule 11 the waiver’s knowing-and-voluntary character and its plain scope are fixed at the plea colloquy; a later Rule 32(j)(1)(B) advisement—however misleading in context—cannot, without mutual assent, modify a material term of the plea bargain as Ricketts v. Adamson’s contract-like framework indicates. Justice Sotomayor’s due-process concern about insulating future liberty restraints is weighty, yet Garza v. Idaho’s statement that waivers are not “absolute” preserves established exceptions (invalid waiver, breach, lack of authority), not an atextual carveout for any claim styled “due process,” and the waiver here (“any appeal on any ground” except ineffective assistance) is the best evidence of what was relinquished. The administrable rule, consistent with the text and precedent, is to enforce the waiver while leaving defendants to challenge truly unlawful conditions through preserved avenues (e.g., invalid waiver, statutory/constitutional limits on the court’s power, or appropriate postconviction mechanisms). I therefore remain with the Respondent.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan are right that, under Ricketts v. Adamson and Rule 11 practice, a routine Rule 32(j) advisement cannot “modify” a plea agreement absent mutual assent, and Garza does not itself announce an open-ended constitutional exception. But that contract-modification frame does not fully answer the distinct procedural-fairness problem: the sentencing court affirmatively told Hunter he had a right to appeal and then invited the government’s position; the government’s silence in that critical moment reasonably signaled that the court’s advisement was operative, creating at least a due-process-based reliance interest (or, minimally, a forfeiture of the government’s ability to invoke the waiver against this specific appeal). Justice Gorsuch’s point that courts cannot unilaterally rewrite bargains is formally correct, yet my pragmatic focus is on the integrity and reliability of on-the-record sentencing procedures—Rule 32(j) should not function as a trap that affirmatively misleads defendants into thinking appellate review is available while later being used to foreclose it. Given the supervised-release condition’s serious bodily-integrity implications, I would allow the appeal to proceed on the narrow ground that the government cannot enforce the waiver after acquiescing in the judge’s contrary advisement at sentencing.

John Roberts.reasoning: Hunter’s appeal waiver was confirmed as knowing and voluntary under Rule 11, and its plain terms encompass this due-process challenge to a supervised-release condition, so enforcing it respects the plea bargain and promotes stability in federal plea practice. Under Garza v. Idaho, appeal waivers are generally enforceable though not absolute; nothing here places Hunter’s claim in a recognized category that survives a broad waiver (such as ineffective assistance, which the agreement expressly preserves). The district court’s post-sentencing Rule 32(j)(1)(B) advisement that Hunter had a right to appeal—without more—does not nullify or modify the earlier waiver, and treating routine advisements or government silence as rewriting plea agreements would undermine institutional legitimacy and invite strategic uncertainty. A narrow disposition enforcing the waiver avoids announcing a sweeping rule about constitutional challenges to supervised-release conditions while adhering to contract-like plea-agreement principles recognized in Ricketts v. Adamson.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: A plea agreement’s appeal waiver is enforceable according to its text when entered knowingly and voluntarily under Rule 11, and nothing in the Constitution’s original meaning suggests a freestanding right to appeal that cannot be waived. Garza v. Idaho recognizes that waivers are not “monolithic” and that a defendant may still contest the waiver’s validity, but it does not hold that a routine post-sentencing advisement about a right to appeal nullifies an earlier, Rule 11-confirmed waiver or expands appellate jurisdiction. The district judge’s later statement—especially absent any express modification of the plea agreement—cannot alter the parties’ bargain, and due-process objections to supervised-release conditions are the sort of sentencing-related claims a broad waiver can cover. Consistent with Ricketts v. Adamson, courts should hold parties to their plea bargains unless the waiver itself is shown unknowing, involuntary, or otherwise invalid, which is not established merely by an unobjected-to standard advisement.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: A knowing and voluntary appellate waiver confirmed during the Rule 11 colloquy is ordinarily enforceable according to its text, and nothing in Rule 11 or Rule 32(j)(1)(B) authorizes a district court to unilaterally alter a bargained-for plea term at sentencing. The judge’s later, routine statement that the defendant has a right to appeal—especially when the defendant in fact retained only limited appellate rights under the agreement—does not constitute mutual assent to modify the waiver under contract-like plea principles recognized in Ricketts v. Adamson, nor does the government’s silence amount to forfeiture of its ability to invoke the waiver on appeal. Permitting defendants to evade broad waivers based on such post-plea advisements would undermine plea bargaining’s stability and impose serious practical costs on the criminal justice system, while still leaving defendants protected by the familiar exceptions (e.g., ineffective assistance) and any explicit carveouts in the waiver’s text.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: A broad appeal waiver cannot be treated as an absolute bar where the defendant raises a due-process challenge to a supervised-release condition that will govern future liberty interests; Garza v. Idaho recognized that “no appeal waiver serves as an absolute bar to all appellate claims,” leaving room for constitutional exceptions that prevent unjust, unreviewable restraints. Enforcing this waiver to foreclose review of an allegedly unconstitutional supervised-release condition risks insulating unlawful deprivations of liberty from any appellate check, contrary to basic due-process norms. Moreover, when the sentencing judge affirmatively told the defendant he had a right to appeal and the government did not object, that post-plea advisement reasonably undermines the clarity and practical enforceability of the waiver under Rule 11’s insistence on knowing and voluntary relinquishment. Given the real-world stakes for a defendant’s post-custody freedom, fairness requires allowing appellate review at least for the due-process claim.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The waiver’s text is sweeping—barring “any appeal on any ground” except ineffective assistance—and Rule 11’s plea colloquy confirmed it was knowing and voluntary, so petitioner’s due-process challenge to a supervised-release condition falls within the waiver’s plain scope. Garza v. Idaho recognizes appeal waivers are not absolute, but it does not create an open-ended constitutional exception; rather, it preserves narrow categories (e.g., invalid waiver, breach, or proceedings beyond the court’s power), none of which is shown here. The judge’s later, routine advisement that petitioner had a “right to appeal,” without more, cannot rewrite or nullify the parties’ bargain under contract-like plea principles (Ricketts v. Adamson), especially where it occurred after the waiver was executed and accepted. Enforcing the waiver as written promotes workability and coherence in plea bargaining while leaving intact the established safety valves for involuntary waivers or unlawful sentences.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: A knowing-and-voluntary appellate waiver confirmed in a Rule 11 colloquy is enforceable according to its plain terms, and nothing in Rule 32(j)(1)(B)’s routine notice at sentencing authorizes a district court unilaterally to rewrite a plea agreement or expand appellate rights beyond what the parties bargained for. Contract-like plea principles recognized in Ricketts v. Adamson support holding both sides to the agreement absent mutual assent to modification, and the government’s silence to a generic “right to appeal” statement cannot supply that assent or overcome Rule 11’s limits on judicial alteration of plea terms. Nor does Garza v. Idaho undermine enforceability of waivers; it concerns counsel’s duty to file a notice of appeal despite a waiver, not whether an otherwise valid waiver bars merits review. Because the waiver here broadly covers “any appeal” (save ineffective assistance), it bars petitioner’s due-process challenge to a supervised-release condition.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: A knowing-and-voluntary appellate waiver confirmed at the Rule 11 colloquy is generally enforceable according to ordinary plea-agreement principles, and nothing in Rule 32(j)’s routine end-of-sentencing advisement authorizes a district court to unilaterally rewrite the parties’ bargain. The sentencing judge’s later statement that the defendant has a “right to appeal,” even if overbroad and unobjected-to, does not negate the earlier, valid waiver or constitute a mutual modification of the plea agreement, which is governed by contract-like principles recognized in Ricketts v. Adamson. Nor does the mere fact that the challenge is framed in due-process terms categorically place it outside a broad waiver that expressly covers appeals “on any ground” other than ineffective assistance; Garza v. Idaho underscores that waivers do not erase all appellate rights, but it does not undermine enforcing a valid waiver to bar a covered appeal. Enforcing the waiver also serves practical workability and institutional interests by honoring settled plea-bargaining expectations and maintaining uniform administration of Rule 11 agreements.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: A knowing and voluntary appellate-rights waiver confirmed during the Rule 11 colloquy is enforceable according to its text, and nothing in Rule 32(j)(1)(B)’s post-sentencing advisement authorizes a district court to unilaterally alter the parties’ bargain. Under contract-like principles governing plea agreements, modification requires mutual assent; a routine, generalized statement at sentencing that the defendant has a “right to appeal,” even if imperfect, does not negate or rewrite an express waiver, nor does the government’s silence amount to forfeiture of the waiver’s enforcement. This approach is consistent with this Court’s treatment of plea agreements as binding bargains (Ricketts v. Adamson) and with recognizing that waivers may coexist with limited appellate rights (Garza v. Idaho). Because Hunter’s due-process attack on a supervised-release condition falls within the waiver’s broad terms and is not among the reserved exceptions, the Fifth Circuit properly dismissed the appeal.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: An appeal waiver is enforceable only if it is knowing and voluntary under Rule 11, and due process requires that defendants be able to rely on clear, on-the-record judicial advisements about their appellate rights at sentencing. When the sentencing judge expressly told Hunter he had a right to appeal and then invited the government’s response, the government’s silence reasonably signaled acquiescence—triggering ordinary waiver/forfeiture principles and undermining the fairness of later invoking the waiver to bar review. Given the severe liberty and bodily-integrity consequences of a supervised-release condition requiring compliance with prescribed psychotropic medication, procedural fairness counsels against treating broad waivers as nearly absolute and against insulating such due-process challenges from any appellate check. Consistent with Garza v. Idaho’s recognition that an appeal waiver does not eliminate all appellate rights and that courts must take a practical, defendant-protective view of waiver consequences, I would vacate and remand to allow appellate consideration of the due-process challenge.
